analysis.one_liner: Sets a federal floor of collective bargaining rights for state and local government workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote; it sat in the Senate labor committee until the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Federal Labor Relations Authority to check whether each state's laws give its government workers basic union rights — the right to organize, join a union chosen by coworkers, bargain over wages and working conditions, and resolve disputes through binding arbitration. States that fall short would come under federal rules that guarantee those rights, with enforcement in federal courts. To protect public safety, it bans strikes and lockouts that would disrupt emergency or police services.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly one-third of state and local government workers who live in states where the law does not give them the right to bargain collectively would gain federally guaranteed organizing and bargaining rights, payroll deduction of union dues, and binding arbitration to settle disputes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public employees in states without bargaining rights

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Federal Labor Relations Authority to determine, for each state, whether state law 'substantially provides' a federal minimum set of rights: self-organization, forming or joining a union, bargaining collectively through a chosen representative, and concerted activity including joint legal claims [S3].

In states that fall short, the Authority must issue and administer rules establishing those rights within two years, including supervising union elections, requiring employers to recognize and bargain with unions, and providing grievance procedures that end in binding arbitration [S3].

Workers would get payroll deduction of union dues, and a private right of action letting workers or unions sue state officials in federal court to enforce compliance, with attorneys' fees available [S3].

The bill protects public safety by prohibiting employers, emergency services workers, and law enforcement officers from lockouts or strikes that would measurably disrupt emergency or public safety services [S2] [S3].
States whose laws already meet the standard keep their own systems, and small towns (fewer than 5,000 people or fewer than 25 public employees) can be exempted at the state's request [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments would bear the cost of negotiating contracts, binding arbitration awards, and likely higher wages and benefits in states that currently restrict bargaining; taxpayers in those states would ultimately fund the difference. States would also give up some control over their own labor policy to a federal agency.
analysis.who_pays_short: State and local governments and their taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Binding arbitration would force state and local governments into contract outcomes they cannot walk away from, which in states with tight budgets could mean higher payroll costs for taxpayers or cuts elsewhere [S3].

The bill inserts a federal agency into what has traditionally been state law: the Federal Labor Relations Authority, which now handles only federal workers, would write and enforce the bargaining rules for any state judged to fall short, a significant shift of authority away from state legislatures [S2] [S3].

Supporters of state control argue that bargaining rules should reflect each state's budget and priorities rather than a single national standard, and that mandatory arbitration can tie elected officials' hands on spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large for the workers it covers: in states with no collective bargaining law for public employees, workers currently have little legal recourse and no enforced contract. The main cost is fiscal — binding arbitration and bargaining in cost-heavy states would raise public payrolls, paid by taxpayers — and a genuine federalism tradeoff, since a federal agency would override state labor rules. Whether the benefits justify the costs depends largely on how states value stable labor relations versus budget control.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mazie Hirono introduced the bill on June 25, 2019, with 40 original cosponsors — 39 Democrats and one Independent — all members of the Senate's Democratic caucus [S1] [S3] [S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
The action history shows no further activity — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — for the remaining 18 months of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public employers in states that restrict union bargaining — and the taxpayers of those states — are better off because the bill never advanced, since they would have faced federal bargaining mandates and binding arbitration. Public employees in those states remain without federally guaranteed bargaining rights.

sides.party_line_note: All 40 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent who caucuses with them, and no Republican cosponsor ever joined; with Republicans controlling the Senate and its committee schedule, the bill never advanced beyond referral [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would create union members and dues-paying roles in roughly half the states that lack full public-sector bargaining laws, and guarantees dues payroll deduction. For the workers themselves, union representation is the direct vehicle for the rights the bill provides.

industries.industry: State and local governments as employers
industries.note: Governments would be required to recognize and bargain with unions and accept binding arbitration, raising labor costs and limiting budget flexibility. Some of that cost would flow to taxpayers, though it buys workers enforceable contracts and a dispute process.

The agency, which currently oversees federal employees, would become the permanent administrator of bargaining rights in any state judged to fall short, with rulemaking, election supervision, subpoena, and enforcement powers.
